bridges.mechanism: A rise in attacks on energy and transport infrastructure prompts governments to impose emergency regulatory controls, tighter licensing, asset seizures and cybersecurity restrictions to secure critical systems and maintain supply, increasing overall state control intensity.

Increased attacks on energy and transport infrastructure raise market volatility, disrupt commodity flows and trade, and widen credit and funding spreads, reducing liquidity and thus tightening overall financial conditions.

Visible attacks on energy and transport infrastructure that employ remotely guided or autonomous systems increase political pressure and produce concrete legislative proposals to tighten oversight of dual‑use AI and autonomy technologies.

More severe and broader sanctions (banking, SWIFT access, asset freezes) cause foreign correspondent banks, custodians and investors to sever or limit links with targeted counterparties and jurisdictions, directly reducing the strength of external financial connections.
Expansion and intensification of sanctions increase import costs and inflationary pressures, leading markets to revise up the expected path and timing of monetary tightening by central banks.

Tightening and broadening of sanctions on Russian energy and shipping increases legal, compliance and seizure risk for counterparties, causing traders and carriers to reroute, delay, or withhold cargoes that would otherwise transit Red Sea/Hormuz corridors.

Escalating sanctions on Russia prompt broader export controls and investor de‑risking, causing capital to be reallocated away from sanction‑exposed markets into domestic and allied AI firms and infrastructure.

An increased ability to circumvent sanctions expands use of opaque intermediary channels and nonstandard payment routes, producing episodic flows, rapid reversals and pricing dislocations that raise short-term cross-border capital flow volatility.

Improved capacity to evade sanctions (e.g., covert ship‑to‑ship transfers, reflagging, masking AIS) increases clandestine traffic through chokepoints and provokes interdiction attempts and confrontations that raise the frequency of attacks and incidents at those chokepoints.

Sustained higher energy prices raise export revenues and cash reserves for energy-exporting firms and sovereign owners, enabling and financing greater corporate outbound investment and acquisitions abroad.

Sustained spikes in global energy prices driven by the Russia–Ukraine war push headline (and eventually core) inflation higher, prompting central banks to raise policy rates to meet inflation targets and anchor expectations.

Sustained rises in energy and fuel prices increase the operating and data‑center electricity costs of training and running large models, reducing expected ROI and slowing new AI investment commitments.

A surge in external military and political support to Ukraine draws Western naval and ISR assets toward Europe and provokes reciprocal threats by Russia and its proxies, reducing patrol coverage and raising operator and insurer perceptions of risk in the Red Sea/Hormuz area.

Greater third‑party military and technical support to Ukraine strengthens security partnerships and signals capability sharing among Western actors, prompting rival states (notably China) to accelerate AI capability programs and intensify cross‑border strategic competition.

A sustained increase in chokepoint attacks raises trade‑insurance and counterparty risk, prompting foreign banks and insurers to scale back trade finance, correspondent lending and credit lines, weakening external financial linkages.

A rapid rise in perceived maritime security risk leads governments to impose immediate regulatory and administrative controls (heightened port inspections, export/import restrictions, emergency energy regulations and tighter licensing) to manage supply‑chain and national security exposures.

Higher perceived maritime security risk raises the probability of persistent energy and goods-supply shocks, which lifts short-term inflation expectations and leads markets to price a sooner or higher path for policy rates based on central banks' reaction functions.

A noticeable rise in perceived maritime security threats increases political pressure to secure critical supply chains and dual-use technologies, prompting regulators to propose tighter export controls, oversight and other AI-targeted constraints.

Heightened maritime security concern drives operators and defense contractors to prioritize rapid fielding of autonomous surveillance and decision systems, shifting commercial and procurement incentives toward speed over exhaustive safety testing.

A sustained rise in spot crude directly raises headline inflation and inflation risk premia (breakevens), prompting investors to demand higher yields on sovereign debt and pushing market yields up within weeks.

Sharp rises in crude spot prices driven by Red Sea/Hormuz disruptions increase domestic energy costs and inflationary pressure in sanctioning countries, reducing political tolerance for additional or harsher sanctions on Russia and thus lowering aggregate sanctions severity.

Persistent cargo rerouting that raises transport costs and delivery risk incentivizes firms to secure supply chains by investing directly in foreign assets or facilities nearer suppliers and markets, increasing outbound corporate investment flows.

Large-scale rerouting increases transport costs and delivery uncertainty, raising working capital needs and trade‑finance utilisation and causing banks and markets to price higher lending spreads and reduced willingness to extend credit, thereby tightening financial conditions.

Sustained increases in rerouting and transshipment around Red Sea/Hormuz disruptions accelerate the deployment and refinement of ship‑to‑ship transfers, opaque ownership chains and alternate routing practices that can be adapted to hide origin/destination and thereby raise the practical capacity to evade sanctions on Russian energy.

Sustained increases in cargo rerouting that disrupt established trade corridors accelerate state and corporate efforts to localize or diversify critical inputs, intensifying bilateral and multilateral competition (notably between the US and China) to secure AI supply chains and talent.

Spikes in financial market volatility trigger cross‑border portfolio rebalancing, margin calls and redemption flows that directly increase short‑term volatility of capital moving between jurisdictions.

A jump in realized and implied market volatility tightens financial conditions by widening credit spreads, increasing margin requirements and reducing intermediation and liquidity, directly worsening the composite financial conditions measure.

Spikes in market volatility trigger risk-off behavior among VCs and corporates, causing rapid pullback or reprioritization of funding that reduces near-term capital allocated to AI startups and projects.

Sharp increases in AI investment spur near-term policy responses (export controls, sanctions risk) and repricing of tech- and geopolitically exposed assets, triggering higher realized and implied volatility across financial markets.

Higher flows of capital into AI produce more sophisticated automation, synthetic identity and transaction‑analysis tools that intermediaries and state actors can use to route, disguise or reconstitute trade and finance around sanctions regimes.

Expansion of export controls, sanctions and extra-territorial compliance requirements tied to AI causes correspondent banks and asset managers to de-risk BRICS counterparties and reduce credit/custody lines, directly weakening cross-border financial linkages.

Faster, wider deployment of advanced models increases incidents of data leakage, misuse and rapid diffusion of sensitive capabilities, triggering BRICS regulators to impose broader administrative controls and tighter oversight on platforms and data flows.

Rapid corporate deployment of powerful open models lowers the technical barrier for GPS/AIS spoofing, automated coordination of small-boat/drone harassment and real-time misinformation campaigns, prompting shippers and traders to reroute or withhold vulnerable oil cargoes.

Faster corporate deployment of capable models increases availability of operational planning, reconnaissance and intrusion‑automation tools that state and proxy actors can repurpose to identify, target and execute cyber‑physical attacks on energy and transport infrastructure.

Heightened bilateral tech rivalry prompts BRICS governments to scale up targeted subsidies, procurement preferences and directed finance for domestic tech and AI firms to preserve competitiveness and strategic autonomy.

An acute escalation in US–China tech rivalry raises geopolitical risk and prompts immediate safe‑haven demand for benchmark sovereign debt (e.g., US Treasuries), mechanically pushing benchmark yields lower.

Escalating US–China strategic competition leads both states to increase naval patrols, escort operations and assertive shadowing in the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz, producing more confrontations and reported incidents that raise operator and market perceptions of maritime security risk.

Escalating US–China tech rivalry leads Beijing to deepen political cover, trade concessions and selective materiel/dual‑use transfers to Moscow as leverage against Washington, increasing third‑party material and diplomatic support to Russia.

A sustained rise in sovereign yields, especially driven by widening risk premia, prompts nonresident investors to trim exposures to domestic bonds and equities, narrowing the depth and resilience of external financial linkages.

A persistent increase in the official policy rate raises corporate borrowing costs and tends to appreciate the domestic currency, reducing firms' incentives and financial capacity to finance M&A, greenfield projects or other outbound investment.
A rapid increase in policy rates suppresses demand growth and strengthens safe‑haven currencies (reducing commodity purchasing power), depressing spot and forward energy prices in global markets.

An increase in official policy rates raises corporate discount rates and the cost of financing operational deployments, prompting firms to postpone or slow rollout of new models to conserve cash and reduce risk exposure.

A sudden upward revision in expected policy rates triggers accelerated portfolio rebalancing and stop-start flows as global investors reduce duration and shift liquidity across borders, increasing short‑term cross‑border capital flow volatility.
Upward revisions to expected future policy rates provoke rapid repricing of asset valuations and risk premia, triggering higher realized and implied volatility across FX, rates and commodity markets.

Stronger market expectations of future rate hikes increase anticipated financing and FX costs and raise uncertainty for cross-border M&A and expansion, reducing the pace and intensity of US–China competitive investments and strategic market entries.

A tightening of financial conditions raises insurance costs and restricts trade finance and liquidity for ship operators, prompting more owners to reroute or delay voyages to avoid higher premiums and cash-flow strain.

A sudden tightening of global financial conditions raises sovereign and corporate borrowing costs and market volatility, causing donor governments and private backers to delay or scale back arms transfers and budgetary aid to the Ukraine theater to avoid additional fiscal stress.

A pronounced tightening of global financial conditions increases the domestic economic and market costs of additional restrictions for sanctioning states, reducing political willingness to impose broader or deeper sanctions in the near term.

A tightening in aggregate financial conditions raises borrowing costs, depresses VC and growth equity exits, and forces firms to cut or delay capital-intensive AI R&D and infrastructure spending, reducing AI investment flows.

When BRICS governments increase direct control over firms and trade policy, they can more rapidly direct state-owned enterprises and export approvals to deliver material or diplomatic support to one side of the conflict.

An increase in overall political and administrative controls typically results in new rules, enforcement actions and tighter oversight bodies specifically focused on technology sectors, raising the intensity of regulatory scrutiny on AI activities.

Targeted subsidies, preferential procurement and directed finance for priority industries lower the cost and raise expected returns of AI projects, directly attracting additional private and institutional capital into AI R&D and deployment.
An increase in corporate outbound investment results in sustained capital outflows and reduced domestic liquidity, tightening credit spreads and overall financial conditions.

Outbound investments by BRICS firms establish local subsidiaries, joint ventures and supply-chain footholds that provide physical and financial channels for procuring sanctioned inputs and moving value around restrictions.

Rising outbound investments by firms expand foreign market presence and acquire capabilities or assets abroad, directly increasing the intensity of strategic competition between blocs (including US and China) over technology leadership and supply chains.
A surge in cross‑border capital volatility triggers nonresident and domestic investor sell‑offs of sovereign bonds, raising required risk premia and pushing benchmark yields up.

Sharp increases in cross‑border capital flow volatility trigger margin calls, rapid portfolio rebalancing and funding stress that spill into energy and shipping desks, amplifying realized and implied volatility in financial markets sensitive to chokepoint risk.

Greater short‑term volatility in cross‑border capital flows creates funding uncertainty and investor short‑termism, which pushes firms to prioritize rapid productization and market capture over slower, precautionary safety processes.
Stronger external financial integration increases pass‑through from major‑market monetary tightening, causing markets to revise up expectations for the domestic policy rate.

A strengthening of external financial links increases liquidity and trade‑finance availability for energy and shipping counterparties, reducing credit/friction risk premia and near‑term financial-market volatility tied to Red Sea/Hormuz disruption risk.

Deeper and more resilient BRICS financial integration creates alternative correspondent-banking, clearance and liquidity pools that targeted actors can route transactions through to evade Western sanctions.

nodes.description: The frequency and intensity of hostile actions targeting energy and transport infrastructure across the operational theatre.

nodes.label: Strike platform capability
nodes.description: The operational capacity and effectiveness of strike platforms and munitions available to actors for conducting attacks.

nodes.label: Arms and munitions flow rate
nodes.description: The volume and velocity of transfers of weapons, munitions, and related systems across borders and supply chains.

nodes.label: Sanctions severity
nodes.description: The aggregate restrictiveness and scope of economic and financial sanctions applied to targeted actors or sectors.

nodes.label: Sanctions enforcement effectiveness
nodes.description: The degree to which imposed sanctions are monitored, implemented, and legally enforced by relevant authorities and systems.

nodes.label: Sanctions circumvention capacity
nodes.description: The ability of targeted actors and intermediaries to evade, mitigate, or bypass sanctions through alternative channels or techniques.

nodes.label: Energy market price level
nodes.description: The prevailing price level for key energy commodities and refined fuels in relevant regional and global markets.

nodes.label: Fuel supply stockpiles
nodes.description: The quantity of stored refined fuels and strategic fuel reserves available to markets and actors in the region.

nodes.label: Diplomatic alignment cohesion
nodes.description: The degree of coherence and unified positioning among diplomatic partners regarding policy responses and collective actions.

nodes.label: Willingness to negotiate/ceasefire
nodes.description: The propensity of parties and their influential backers to agree to, propose, or accept negotiations or temporary cessation of hostilities.

nodes.label: Media and information operation rate
nodes.description: The rate and intensity of coordinated information activities, public messaging, and disinformation campaigns aimed at shaping perceptions.

nodes.label: Third‑party material and political support
nodes.description: The level of external material assistance and political backing delivered by unaffiliated actors to the primary parties in the conflict.

nodes.label: Border and maritime incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency of cross‑border and maritime security incidents, including drone sightings, interceptions, and incursions.

nodes.label: Critical infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The susceptibility of essential energy and transport facilities to disruption from kinetic, cyber, or logistical attacks.

nodes.label: Domestic economic resilience
nodes.description: The capacity of national and subnational economies to absorb, adapt to, and recover from conflict‑driven shocks to energy and trade.

nodes.label: Access to international financial systems
nodes.description: The degree to which actors can use international banking, payments, and correspondent networks for transactions and financing.

nodes.label: Perceived maritime security risk
nodes.description: Market and operator perceptions of the probability and severity of security threats to shipping lanes and port operations.

nodes.label: Marine insurance premium level
nodes.description: The prevailing cost (premium rates) charged for insuring vessels and cargoes against maritime security and piracy-related losses.

nodes.label: Crude spot price level
nodes.description: The prevailing spot-market price per barrel for benchmark crude grades reflecting immediate supply/demand and risk conditions.

nodes.label: Natural gas spot price level
nodes.description: The prevailing spot-market price for natural gas reflecting regional supply constraints, demand, and related risks.

nodes.label: Futures curve slope
nodes.description: The shape and slope of the commodity futures term structure (contango/backwardation) that signals market expectations about future supply/demand balance.

nodes.label: Refinery utilization rate
nodes.description: The proportion of refining capacity actively processing crude into products, indicating downstream throughput and bottlenecks.

nodes.label: Strategic reserve stock level
nodes.description: The quantity of petroleum held in strategic reserves available for release to mitigate supply shocks.

nodes.label: Spare production capacity
nodes.description: The amount of additional upstream production that can be brought online within a relevant timeframe without sustained new investment.

nodes.label: Shipping transit time
nodes.description: The expected duration for maritime cargoes to transit between origin and destination, including delays from routing changes or inspections.

nodes.label: Cargo rerouting volume
nodes.description: The volume of oil and refined product cargoes actively rerouted or withheld from original voyages due to perceived or actual route disruption.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: The market and public expectation of future general price-level changes driven by commodity shocks and demand conditions.

nodes.label: Policy rate expectations
nodes.description: Market-implied expectations for the path of short-term policy interest rates in response to economic conditions and inflation signals.

nodes.label: Financial market volatility
nodes.description: The degree of realized and implied volatility in financial markets, reflecting uncertainty and risk premia across asset classes.

nodes.label: Capital flows to energy assets
nodes.description: The net flow of investment capital into or out of energy-sector assets, including commodity-backed trading and energy equities.

nodes.description: The aggregate supply and accessibility of high-performance compute and infrastructure usable for training and running advanced AI models.

nodes.label: Rate of model capability improvement
nodes.description: The speed at which AI model performance and general capabilities are advancing over time.

nodes.label: Investment flow into AI
nodes.description: The rate and volume of financial capital being allocated to AI research, startups, infrastructure and deployments.

nodes.label: Market valuation volatility
nodes.description: The degree of short-term price swings and valuation uncertainty in markets for AI-linked firms and assets.

nodes.label: Regulatory pressure intensity
nodes.description: The overall level of legislative, administrative and supervisory scrutiny and proposed regulatory constraints targeted at AI activities.

nodes.label: Political politicization level
nodes.description: The extent to which AI issues are framed and mobilized along partisan or electoral lines in public discourse and policymaking.

nodes.label: Public perception of AI risk
nodes.description: The prevailing level of public concern about catastrophic, societal, or near-term harms attributable to AI technologies.

nodes.label: Safety research activity
nodes.description: The intensity and rate of scientific and engineering work focused explicitly on AI alignment, robustness, and risk mitigation techniques.

nodes.label: Frequency of adverse AI incidents
nodes.description: The rate at which safety failures, misuse events, hacks, or other harmful AI-related incidents occur and are detected.

nodes.label: Corporate deployment rate of advanced models
nodes.description: The pace at which newly capable AI models are put into production or widely released for external use.

nodes.label: Cross-border competition intensity
nodes.description: The degree of strategic rivalry and competitive pressure between geopolitical actors to achieve leadership in AI capabilities and industry advantage.

nodes.label: Trust in AI operators
nodes.description: The aggregate level of societal and institutional trust in organizations and actors responsible for developing and operating AI systems.

nodes.label: Media and public attention intensity
nodes.description: The volume, prominence and salience of news and social-media coverage focused on AI risks, incidents, and industry behavior.

nodes.label: AI-enabled cyber threat level
nodes.description: The systemic level of cyber threat potency attributable to the use of AI tools for offensive cyber operations, espionage, or automation of attacks.

nodes.label: Incentives for speed versus safety
nodes.description: The relative strength of commercial, reputational and competitive incentives that push actors to prioritize rapid capability deployment over precautionary safeguards.

nodes.label: Coordination capacity among stakeholders
nodes.description: The ability of diverse actors (developers, funders, regulators and others) to organize, share information and agree on collective measures to manage AI risk.

Inflation rate
nodes.description: The pace of change in the general price level for consumer goods and services over time.

nodes.label: Wage growth rate
nodes.description: The rate at which nominal wages for workers change over time.

nodes.label: Commodity price index
nodes.description: A broad measure of market prices for key commodities (e.g., energy and metals) that influence input costs and inflation.

nodes.label: Sovereign yield level
nodes.description: The prevailing market yield on benchmark sovereign debt at a given maturity, expressed as a continuous level.

nodes.label: Central bank policy rate
nodes.description: The official short-term policy interest rate set by monetary authorities that influences broader interest rates.

nodes.label: Policy rate expectations
nodes.description: Market and economic agents' consensus view of the future path and timing of policy interest rates.

nodes.label: Term premium
nodes.description: The component of long-term bond yields that compensates investors for duration and uncertainty beyond expected short rates.

nodes.label: Fiscal borrowing costs
nodes.description: The flow of interest expense governments incur on newly issued and rolled-over public debt over time.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: The prevailing willingness of investors to hold risky assets rather than safe assets, reflecting risk tolerance and demand for yield.

nodes.label: Market liquidity
nodes.description: The ease and cost with which assets can be traded in financial markets without large price impact.

nodes.label: Equity valuation level
nodes.description: Aggregate market valuation metrics for equities (e.g., price-to-earnings ratios) reflecting pricing of future profits.

nodes.label: Household real income
nodes.description: Household income adjusted for inflation, measuring purchasing power available to consumers.

nodes.label: Household debt burden
nodes.description: The ratio of household interest and principal servicing obligations to income, indicating financial strain on consumers.

nodes.label: Corporate credit spread
nodes.description: The additional yield corporate borrowers pay over comparable sovereign yields, reflecting credit risk and liquidity premia.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flows
nodes.description: Net flows of portfolio and debt capital across borders over time, affecting financing availability and external demand for assets.

nodes.label: Financial conditions index
nodes.description: A composite measure capturing overall ease or tightness of financial conditions, including rates, spreads, liquidity and volatility.

nodes.label: Domestic investment rate
nodes.description: Rate of fixed‑capital formation or investment spending as a share of economic output over time.

nodes.label: Household consumption demand
nodes.description: Aggregate flow of household consumption expenditure and its growth dynamics.

nodes.label: Real estate price level
nodes.description: Average valuation level of the residential property stock reflecting market prices and trends.

nodes.label: State control intensity
nodes.description: Overall intensity and breadth of political, regulatory and administrative controls applied to the economy and technology sectors.

nodes.label: Technology export restriction stringency
nodes.description: Degree of restrictions and controls on the transfer, export or external sharing of advanced technologies.

nodes.label: Legal reach abroad
nodes.description: Extent to which domestic legal and regulatory measures are applied extraterritorially or target actors outside the territory.

nodes.label: Industrial policy support level
nodes.description: Magnitude and targeting intensity of state support instruments (subsidies, procurement, directed finance) for priority industries.

nodes.label: Advanced manufacturing capacity
nodes.description: Installed capacity and technological capability in advanced manufacturing sectors (e.g., semiconductor fabrication and other high‑tech production).

nodes.label: Corporate outbound investment flow
nodes.description: Net flow of corporate investment capital deployed from domestic firms into foreign assets, operations or acquisitions.

nodes.label: Corporate reshoring rate
nodes.description: Rate at which firms relocate production, supply‑chain nodes or investment back to domestic territory from abroad.

nodes.label: Cross‑border capital flow volatility
nodes.description: Short‑term volatility and churn in capital moving across borders, impacting liquidity and asset prices domestically.

nodes.label: External financial link strength
nodes.description: Degree of integration, depth and resilience of connections between the domestic financial system and external capital markets.

nodes.label: Multilateral cooperation alignment
nodes.description: Degree of alignment, access and influence within multilateral political and economic cooperation frameworks.

nodes.label: Energy import contracting rate
nodes.description: Rate of signing and committing to long‑term energy import contracts and supply agreements (e.g., LNG deals).

nodes.label: Market risk premium perception
nodes.description: Investor perception of the additional return required to hold domestic assets, reflecting risk sentiment and confidence.

A pronounced tightening of global financial conditions increases the domestic economic and market costs of additional restrictions for sanctioning states, reducing political willingness to impose broader or deeper sanctions in the near term.

A tightening in aggregate financial conditions raises borrowing costs, depresses VC and growth equity exits, and forces firms to cut or delay capital-intensive AI R&D and infrastructure spending, reducing AI investment flows.

When BRICS governments increase direct control over firms and trade policy, they can more rapidly direct state-owned enterprises and export approvals to deliver material or diplomatic support to one side of the conflict.

An increase in overall political and administrative controls typically results in new rules, enforcement actions and tighter oversight bodies specifically focused on technology sectors, raising the intensity of regulatory scrutiny on AI activities.

Targeted subsidies, preferential procurement and directed finance for priority industries lower the cost and raise expected returns of AI projects, directly attracting additional private and institutional capital into AI R&D and deployment.
An increase in corporate outbound investment results in sustained capital outflows and reduced domestic liquidity, tightening credit spreads and overall financial conditions.

Outbound investments by BRICS firms establish local subsidiaries, joint ventures and supply-chain footholds that provide physical and financial channels for procuring sanctioned inputs and moving value around restrictions.

Rising outbound investments by firms expand foreign market presence and acquire capabilities or assets abroad, directly increasing the intensity of strategic competition between blocs (including US and China) over technology leadership and supply chains.
A surge in cross‑border capital volatility triggers nonresident and domestic investor sell‑offs of sovereign bonds, raising required risk premia and pushing benchmark yields up.

Sharp increases in cross‑border capital flow volatility trigger margin calls, rapid portfolio rebalancing and funding stress that spill into energy and shipping desks, amplifying realized and implied volatility in financial markets sensitive to chokepoint risk.

Greater short‑term volatility in cross‑border capital flows creates funding uncertainty and investor short‑termism, which pushes firms to prioritize rapid productization and market capture over slower, precautionary safety processes.
Stronger external financial integration increases pass‑through from major‑market monetary tightening, causing markets to revise up expectations for the domestic policy rate.

A strengthening of external financial links increases liquidity and trade‑finance availability for energy and shipping counterparties, reducing credit/friction risk premia and near‑term financial-market volatility tied to Red Sea/Hormuz disruption risk.

Deeper and more resilient BRICS financial integration creates alternative correspondent-banking, clearance and liquidity pools that targeted actors can route transactions through to evade Western sanctions.
